title: 道德經 第七十章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 70, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 87. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 70 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 知難 (Hard to Know). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
吾言甚易知，
甚易行。
天下莫能知，
莫能行。

morph.gloss: to put into practice, to carry out (xíng)
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world and everyone in it
none, no one — a negative carrying its own subject

sentences.l:
My words are exceedingly easy to know,
exceedingly easy to practise.
Under heaven none can know,
none can practise.
sentences.i: My words are very easy to understand and very easy to put into practice; yet no one under heaven is able to understand them, no one able to put them into practice.
sentences.n:
易 + a verb is the standing way to say 'easy to ——', and notice which way round it faces: in 易知 the thing understood is the subject and the understander is nowhere in the sentence. Chinese needs no passive marker to do this; position alone does it.

Then notice what is missing from the second half. 莫能知 is bare 'none can know' — know what? The object is simply left out, as objects are all the time in this language once the topic is clear. English has to put 'them' back in.

知 and 行, knowing and doing, are the pair the whole chapter turns on, and they will run through Chinese thought for the next two thousand years. 行 is the same character you have just met read háng in chapter 69's 行無行, 'ranks'; here it is xíng, to walk a thing out, to carry it into practice.

莫 you have met often — chapter 32's 天下莫能臣, chapter 59's 莫若嗇. It is a negative with its subject already inside it, so it needs no noun of its own; 天下 in front of it is the topic, the field it ranges over.

morph.gloss: an ancestor, the founding forebear of a line — the one the whole descent traces back to
a lord, a prince — the one who rules over something

sentences.l:
Words have an ancestor;
affairs have a lord.
sentences.i: What is said has its forebear; what is done has its master.
sentences.n:
Six characters, and both of the images in them are borrowed from outside language altogether: one from the ancestral hall and one from the court. 宗 is the founding ancestor of a clan, the man at the head of the descent; 君 is the prince a state obeys. Words come down from something the way a family comes down from its forebear; deeds answer to something the way subjects answer to a lord.

有 here is 'has', not 'there exists': 言 and 事 are the topics and each is said to have its own governing term. Wang Bi supplies what that term is in both halves, and in both halves it is the ten thousand things he reaches for — 宗 he glosses 萬物之宗, the forebear of the ten thousand things, and 君 he glosses 萬物之主, their master. The chapter never says 道 aloud here; it does not have to.

sentences.t:
夫唯無知，
是以不我知。

morph.gloss: now, as for —— (the sentence-opening particle, read fú; read fū it is the noun 'a grown man')
to be without, there is no
knowing, understanding — also 'cleverness'; see the note
therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither half gives you it alone
me — the object, and it stands BEFORE its verb

sentences.l:
Now, it is only that there is no knowing —
and so they do not me know.
sentences.i: It is precisely because there is no understanding that they fail to understand me.
sentences.n:
夫唯 X, 是以 Y is the book's clinching frame, 'it is precisely because X that Y'. You met it in this exact form in chapter 2 (夫唯弗居，是以不去), and it comes twice more in the next two chapters. The same frame often closes with 故 'therefore' instead — chapters 8, 15 and 22 all do that (夫唯不爭，故無尤).

不我知 is 不知我 with the object pulled in front of the verb, and that is a rule of the language, not a liberty: in a negated clause a pronoun object goes ahead of its verb. You saw the same shape in chapter 9's 莫之能守 and chapter 32's 莫之令. Take the negative away and 我 drops back where English expects it. The literal line keeps the Chinese order so the inversion is visible.

無知 can be cut two ways and the chapter does not settle it. Either there is no understanding abroad in the world — nobody grasps the thing — or, taking 知 in the pejorative sense this book often gives it, 'cleverness', it is precisely because my words have no cleverness in them that no one recognises them. Both readings end in the same place, which may be why the text leaves it alone.

sentences.t:
知我者希，
則我者貴。

morph.gloss: the one who — turns everything before it into a noun
so few as to be barely there; of a sound, too faint to hear
to take as a rule, to pattern oneself on — the noun 'a rule, a standard' working as a verb, not the usual 'then'

sentences.l:
Those who know me are few;
those who take me for their rule are precious.
sentences.i: Few know me; and those who take me for their pattern are the precious ones.
sentences.n:
則 is normally the little word 'then', which is exactly why this line is argued over, and you should know that our English takes a side.

Read 則 as 'then' and the couplet runs 'those who know me being few, I am therefore the prized thing.' Read it as a verb — 則 is also the noun 'a rule, a measuring-line', and this language turns nouns into verbs freely — and 則我者 is 'the ones who take me for their rule', which answers 知我者 word for word. We ship the second, on one grammatical ground: 者 nominalises what stands before it, and what stands before it here is 則我, a verb and its object.

Our own crib leans the other way, and you should hear that plainly. Wang Bi comments 知我益希，我亦無匹 — 'the fewer who know me, the less I have any match' — and that is the 'then' reading: the scarcity of knowers is what makes the speaker precious, and 貴 is said of him, not of them. So the line as printed here departs from Wang Bi's drift, on the parallelism, and you are entitled to hold the other reading.

希 is chapter 14's word — there it named what you listen for and cannot hear. Rarity in this book is always close to inaudibility.

morph.gloss: therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither half gives you it alone
the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a moral saint
to throw over oneself, to wear — read pī here, not bèi; bèi is the other word, the one that marks a passive
coarse hair-cloth — the undyed brown sacking a labourer or a poor man wears
to carry in the fold of the robe, against the breast
jade, the most prized of stones

sentences.l: Therefore the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade in his breast.
sentences.n:
被 is one of the characters that is really two words. Read bèi it is the passive marker of later Chinese; read pī it is this word, to throw a garment over yourself — a sense that was eventually given its own character, 披. The line means wearing, not being worn.

褐 is the cheapest cloth there was, coarse undyed hair or hemp, the standing sign of a poor man in classical texts; 懷 is not vague 'harbouring' but a physical gesture, carrying something in the fold of the robe over the breast, where a man keeps what he will not put down.

And the chapter closes itself. It began by saying the words are easy; it ends with the one who says them dressed like anybody, with the jade out of sight. That is the answer to why no one knows him — there is nothing on the outside to know.
